1 Introduction

Du, Ge and Qiao (2014) estimate how expectations about the renminbi (RMB)–US dollar exchange rate affected the accumulation of China’s foreign exchange reserves (FER) between 2000 and 2011. They split the sample into four exchange-rate regimes and measure expectations in two ways: a forecast generated from a three-stage regression model (Model I) and the 12-month non-deliverable forward rate (NDF, Model II). [YOUR READING: in two or three sentences, the article’s central claim as stated in its abstract and conclusion, quoted or closely paraphrased, with page numbers.]

The question matters because [YOUR READING: why this relation mattered, for example reserve accumulation and sterilisation costs, “hot money” inflows under an expected appreciation, and the policy debate at the time. One paragraph, with two or three references.]

This note is a replication in the sense of the Journal of Comments and Replications in Economics: it assesses the reliability of the article’s claims. We do two things. First, we reproduce the published estimates from the data of the original document on which the article is based, which contains the full dataset and every test and estimation table (Section 4). Second, we correct twelve problems in the original analysis, one at a time, and show how each correction changes the estimated effect of expectations (Sections 5 and 6).

Disclosure. The author of this note is the first author of the original article. To prevent the replication from being steered towards a preferred result, every rule that selects data, specifications or classifications was written down, dated, before the estimates it governs were computed, and the code and results of each step were committed to git. These rules include which balance-of-payments series is used, which unit-root specification, which Model I specification counts as the reproduction, and when an estimate counts as reproduced. Each rule is recorded, with the options considered and the evidence, in a numbered decision log, which Appendix A lists. 2 The original study

2.1 Models

The article estimates two models of the monthly change in reserves, \(\Delta FER_t\), separately in four periods. Model I builds an expected change of the exchange rate in three stages. Stage 1 regresses the change of the exchange rate (RMB per USD) on fundamentals:

\[ \Delta ER_t = b_0 + b_1\,\Delta BOP_t + b_2\,\Delta i_t + b_3\,\Delta \pi_t + b_4\,\Delta GDP_t + x_t . \tag{1}\]

Stage 2 projects the stage-1 result on its own lags, without a constant:

\[ \widehat{\Delta ER}_t = \sum_{s=1}^{j} a_s\,\widehat{\Delta ER}_{t-s} + e_t , \tag{2}\]

and stage 3 uses the fitted value \(\widehat{\widehat{\Delta ER}}_t\) as the expectation:

\[ \Delta FER_t = \tau_0 + \tau_1\,\widehat{\widehat{\Delta ER}}_t + \tau_2\,\Delta NX_t + \tau_3\,\Delta FDB_t + \tau_4\,\Delta FDI_t + y_t . \tag{3}\]

Model II replaces the generated expectation by the observed 12-month NDF:

\[ \Delta FER_t = g_0 + g_1\,\Delta NDF_t + g_2\,\Delta GDP_t + g_3\,\Delta NX_t + g_4\,\Delta FDB_t + g_5\,\Delta FDI_t + w_t . \tag{4}\]

The variables are defined in Table 2. In the original document, the regressions of Periods 1 and 3 have AR(1) errors (ARIMA(1,1,0)) and those of Periods 2 and 4 are estimated by OLS. The periods follow the exchange-rate regime (Table 1).

3 Data

3.1 The original data

All data and all reproduction targets are read by code from the original document; nothing is transcribed by hand. Appendix I of the original document supplies nine monthly variables for the 144 months from January 2000 to December 2011 (Table 2). The extracted data were checked against the original study’s descriptive statistics (Tables 3.2 to 3.9): of the 304 cells of those tables, 267 agree to the printed decimals on the raw data (decision W2-13; tolerance: half a unit of the last printed digit, W2-07). [YOUR READING: how the remaining cells are explained, from W2-13: for example the Period 1 correlations involving the constant exchange rate.]

3.2 Inputs not in the original appendix

Two regressors are not in the appendix and were collected anew, and price data were added for the corrections (Table 3; State Administration of Foreign Exchange (2026); Wind Information Co. (2026); International Monetary Fund (2026); Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (2026); National Bureau of Statistics of China (2026)).

  • Balance of payments. The quarterly current account (SAFE, BPM6 presentation) is converted to months. Of three candidate conversions (quarterly value held, divided by three, year-to-date), the one used, bop_ca_ytd, was chosen by a rule fixed before any Model I estimate. The rule combines the distance to the original unit-root statistic and to the four stage-1 Durbin–Watson statistics (W2-01, W2-10, W2-12).1
  • NDF. The 12-month USD/CNY NDF is the only Wind tenor that covers 2000–2011. Month-end and month-average versions of the daily series were compared with the original unit-root statistic before Model II was estimated; the version used is ndf_mend (W2-06, W2-10).
  • Consumer prices. For the deflator correction (Section 5.6), a fixed-base consumer price index for China was taken from the IMF data portal and cross-checked against FRED (OECD data). The NBS published year-on-year index (same month of the previous year = 100) was used to identify the original study’s inflation series (W4-05, W4-14).

4 Reproduction

4.1 Procedure

The reproduction follows rules fixed before estimation. Because the original document does not fully document Model I, all twelve combinations of its undocumented choices were estimated. These choices are whether stage 2 projects the stage-1 fitted values or the observed exchange rate, the number of lags (one to three), and whether the variables are used as published or divided by \(\pi/100\), as the article states. The combination that reproduces most published cells was then named the headline (W3-02). Each estimate is classified on its sign and star level only (W1-07), with the meanings of the marks taken from the notes of the original tables and significance meaning p < 0.10. An estimate is reproduced if it has the same sign and the same star level as the published one, or if both are insignificant; partially reproduced if both are significant with the same sign but a different star level; and not reproduced if significance flips, or if the signs differ and either estimate is significant. Magnitude, measured as the gap in published standard errors, is reported but does not affect the class. First differences are taken on the whole 2000–2011 series (the “full” convention, W3-01); differencing within each period is reported as a sensitivity check.

4.2 Unit-root tests

The article reports augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) tests; the original tables report DF-GLS tests (Elliott et al. 1996). The original document does not state its lag rule. The specification that best reproduces the original statistics of the eight appendix variables was selected and then fixed (W2-02, W2-09). Table 4 shows the original statistics, our DF-GLS statistics and the ADF statistics at the same lag. DF-GLS and ADF agree on rejection at 5% in 14 of 14 series. [YOUR READING: how close our DF-GLS statistics are to the original study’s (compare the first two columns), and whether any stationarity judgement differs.]

a Original DF-GLS: original Tables 4.1 (levels) and 4.2 (first differences). Our DF-GLS and ADF use the specification fixed in Week 2 (deflated/trend/common/fixed_1) and the same number of lags.
b Critical values at 5%: DF-GLS from urca (Elliott, Rothenberg and Stock 1996 tables), ADF from urca (Dickey-Fuller tables). The original’s critical values (Stata dfgls, finite-sample) differ by construction; compare the statistics.

4.4 Autocorrelation tests

The original study tests residual autocorrelation with the Durbin–Watson statistic and, where it is inconclusive, with the Breusch–Godfrey test (original Tables 4.3 to 4.8). Over all tables, data versions and conventions, 1 of 168 statistics agree with the printed values to the printed decimals, and 124 of 168 test decisions agree (W3-12). On deflated data under the primary convention, the decisions agree in 37 of 42 cases. [YOUR READING: what you conclude from statistics that do not reproduce while most decisions do.]

4.5 Chow tests

The original study reports Chow tests of equal coefficients in adjacent periods (original Table 4.11). Table 8 shows them next to three recalculations. In every model and pair, the published F statistic exceeds the largest recalculated one by a factor of at least \(10^{-7.8}\) (W3-13). The published degrees of freedom match those of the same regressions estimated in levels, rather than in differences, in 11 of 12 comparisons. [YOUR READING: what the degrees-of-freedom match suggests about how the published statistics were computed. Mark it as your interpretation.]

a Published: original Table 4.11 as printed.
b Classic: Chow F with a common error variance, on the model as estimated in first differences, and on the same regressors in levels (whose degrees of freedom are compared with the published ones in the text).
c Robust Wald: equality of all coefficients of the two regimes in the fully interacted pooled model (Table 4), Newey-West covariance, F = W/q.

5 Corrections

We take the twelve problems listed in the replication plan one at a time. For each, we state what the original did, why that is a problem, what we do instead, and what changes. The data and model changes are cumulative, and we assess their combined effect in Section 6.

5.1 Standard errors labelled as t-statistics

The article describes the numbers in parentheses below each coefficient as t-statistics. The significance marks printed in the same table allow a direct test. If the parentheses held t-statistics, the marks would follow from those numbers; if they held standard errors, the marks would follow from the ratio of coefficient to parenthesis. Read as standard errors, the parentheses reproduce the printed marks in 42 of 44 cells (95%); read as t-statistics, in 22 (50%). The cells where the standard-error reading does not reproduce the marks are: Model I, Period 1, DER_hathat; Model I, Period 4, DFDB. [YOUR READING: what the numbers in parentheses are, and whether the non-matching cells lie near a significance threshold (corr_relabel.csv, column implied_t_if_se).] Throughout this note, the parentheses of the published tables are treated as standard errors.

5.2 Units: level coefficients and log differences

All variables of 1 to 4 are first differences of levels, so each coefficient is measured in the units of the variables in Table 2, for example reserves per unit change of the exchange rate. [YOUR READING: quote the article’s percentage interpretation of a coefficient, with page, and state why a level coefficient cannot be read as a percentage.] To give the coefficients a unit-free reading, all models were re-estimated with log differences of the strictly positive series (FER, the exchange rate, the NDF, GDP, FDB and FDI). The expectation coefficient then is an elasticity; net exports, the balance of payments, inflation and the interest rate stay in level differences (row 6 of Tables 13 and 14).

5.3 Sign convention

Both expectation measures are quoted in RMB per US dollar, so a rise is an expected depreciation of the RMB. A positive coefficient therefore means that reserves grow faster when a depreciation is expected, and a negative one that they grow faster when an appreciation is expected. YOUR READING: how the article describes the sign in its abstract and conclusion, and whether that description matches this convention. Use the Period 4 Model II coefficient: published sign from 6

5.4 Generated regressors

In Model I, the stage-3 regressor is estimated in stages 1 and 2. The conventional stage-3 standard errors treat it as data and so ignore the sampling variation of the earlier stages (Pagan 1984; Murphy and Topel 1985). A bootstrap of the whole three-stage chain includes that variation. Stages 1 to 3 are re-estimated in each of 999 replications, with seed 20261001 (W4-01). The primary scheme is a wild bootstrap (Mammen 1993; Davidson and Flachaire 2008): the residuals of stage 1 and the innovations of stage 3 are multiplied by the same Rademacher draw in each month, which preserves their correlation, and the AR(1) errors of Periods 1 and 3 are rebuilt from the sign-flipped innovations. A moving-block bootstrap within periods (Künsch 1989) is reported as a check. Every coefficient was estimated in at least 999 of 999 replications.

For the headline specification on deflated data, the ratio of the bootstrap to the conventional standard error of the expectation coefficient is, by period: Period 1 0.55, Period 2 1.18, Period 3 1.02, Period 4 0.79 (wild) and Period 1 1.65, Period 2 2.03, Period 3 1.10, Period 4 2.35 (block). Figure 2 compares the intervals, and Figure 3 shows the bootstrap distributions. YOUR READING: whether the conventional standard errors understate or overstate the uncertainty, and whether any significance mark changes (row 2 of 13

5.5 Year-to-date GDP

In the appendix, the GDP of every month of a quarter is the cumulative GDP of the year to date. Its first difference is therefore zero in two months of each quarter, positive at each quarter start, and strongly negative every January, when the cumulation restarts. This January fall is an accounting artefact that enters both models as a regressor. The correction replaces it by discrete quarterly GDP (the difference of consecutive year-to-date values), held in each month of the quarter (W4-05). The code first verifies that the appendix value is constant within every quarter. The effect is shown in row 3 of Table 13 and Table 14, to be compared with row 1b, the reproduction on the same (raw) data.

5.6 Deflator

The article divides every variable by \(\pi/100\). Here \(\pi\) is the consumer price index with the same month of the previous year = 100, a year-on-year growth factor \(P_t/P_{t-12}\) rather than a price level. Dividing by it gives \(X_t P_{t-12}/P_t\): the real value multiplied by last year’s price level, not a real series. The correction divides the value variables (FER, GDP, net exports, FDI, external debt and the balance of payments) by a fixed-base consumer price index, rebased to 2000 = 100, from the IMF. The exchange rate and the NDF are not deflated: they are prices of one currency in another, and a real exchange rate would require both countries’ price levels (W4-05).2

We check the price data in two ways (Table 9 and Figure 4). First, we compare the original \(\pi\) with the same-month year-on-year index published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS): 144 of 144 months agree within the printed decimals, with a largest gap of 0.000 points (W4-14). [YOUR READING: what this comparison shows about the source of the original \(\pi\).] Second, the year-on-year rates implied by the IMF index agree with the published ones within the printed decimals in 31 of 144 months (largest gap 0.592 points).3 [YOUR READING: from Figure 4, where the gaps between the published and the index-implied rates lie in time. “Our interpretation suggests …” (for example the NBS basket changes; mark as a hypothesis).]

5.7 Period 1: exchange-rate variation

From January 2000 to June 2005 the RMB was pegged to the US dollar, and the appendix exchange rate is constant (standard deviation 0.000 on raw data). Its change is zero, so no expectation effect can be estimated from it: the coefficient is not identified (W3-10). In the article’s deflated data the exchange rate varies (standard deviation 0.138), and that variation comes from the deflator: the \(R^2\) of the deflated exchange-rate change on the change of \(\pi\) is 0.999 (Table 10). A Period 1 “expectation effect” estimated on deflated data is therefore an effect of inflation. With the exchange rate undeflated (the corrected data), the Period 1 coefficient is reported as not identified.

5.8 Unit-root test label

The article reports ADF tests; the original study ran DF-GLS tests. Table 4 reports both at the same lag, and they agree on rejection in 14 of 14 series. This correction relabels the tests and changes no conclusion that depends on them. CONFIRM from 4

5.9 Chow tests, correctly specified

The classic Chow test (Chow 1960) assumes equal error variances in the two regimes and no autocorrelation. Both assumptions are doubtful with monthly data across exchange-rate regimes. The corrected test estimates one regression over 2000–2011 in which every coefficient is regime-specific (Section 5.10), and tests the equality of all coefficients of two adjacent regimes with a Wald test based on Newey–West standard errors (last column of Table 8; Table 11). For the corrected data, Model I, the tests give: regimes 1–2, F(4, 122) = 7.84, p < 0.001; regimes 2–3, F(5, 122) = 4.52, p < 0.001; regimes 3–4, F(5, 122) = 0.80, p = 0.553. For Model II, in the same order: F(6, 119) = 6.50, p < 0.001; F(6, 119) = 12.91, p < 0.001; F(6, 119) = 3.97, p = 0.001. [YOUR READING: whether the regime split of the original is supported, pair by pair.]

5.10 Period 2: pooled model with regime interactions

Period 2 has about a year of monthly observations and five or six regressors, leaving very few residual degrees of freedom. Following the replication plan, the four periods are pooled in one regression with regime-specific constants. In the full variant every coefficient is regime-specific, which gives the same point estimates as the separate regressions but one set of standard errors for the whole sample. In the expectation-only variant only the constant and the expectation term are regime-specific and the controls are common (W4-02). Standard errors are Newey–West, with a lag of 4 (Newey and West 1987, 1994) (W4-03).

The expectation-only variant is valid only if the controls have the same effect in every regime. The Wald test of that restriction in the full model gives F(9, 122) = 3.76, p < 0.001 for Model I and F(12, 119) = 3.55, p < 0.001 for Model II (corrected data). The test that the expectation coefficient is the same in all regimes gives F(2, 122) = 3.33, p = 0.039 (Model I) and F(3, 119) = 1.55, p = 0.206 (Model II). [YOUR READING: whether the equal-controls restriction is rejected, and therefore which of the two pooled variants is the appropriate one; then what the pooled model says about Period 2.]

For reference, the Model II coefficient of Period 4 is -1,294.45* (SE 531.20) as published, -1,282.99* (SE 523.64) in our reproduction, -1,506.26** (SE 482.76) on the corrected data, and -0.460** (SE 0.162) as an elasticity. For Model I, Period 3, it is -200.07 (SE 476.61) as published, 462.55 (SE 1,016.05) reproduced, and -2,871.44 (SE 2,699.49) corrected, with a wild-bootstrap standard error of 1,558.61 (p = 0.318).

7 Reproducibility and data availability

Every result in this note is produced by the code in the replication package, [REPOSITORY URL], at commit 2447209, with R version 4.5.3 (2026-03-11 ucrt) and the package versions recorded in renv.lock; the tables and figures were generated on 2026-10-06. The code starts from the raw files and runs in a fixed order; each script writes a run log. The bootstrap uses a fixed seed, so reruns give identical draws. [CONFIRM from two 08_corrections logs: a rerun reproduced every estimate and bootstrap standard error.]5

Public data (SAFE, IMF, FRED, NBS) are included in the package with their download dates and checksums (Table 3). Two inputs cannot be redistributed. The original document is unpublished, and its reproduction targets (the numbers of its tables) are [included / withheld; W4-08]. The Wind NDF series is proprietary: a reader with Wind access can export it using the code in Table 3 and run the package unchanged. Without it, everything except Model II and the NDF unit-root test can be rerun. [CONFIRM OR EDIT]
